# Command and Control and Air Mobility in U.S. Air Force Doctrine

## Scope and provenance of this synthesis

This document draws on two Air Force Doctrine Publications: AFDP 3-0.1, *Command and Control*, dated 22 January 2025[^afdp-3-0-1-p1], and AFDP 3-36, *Air Mobility Operations*, dated 24 June 2024[^afdp-3-36-p1]. The two publications address different subject matter but converge on a shared definition of command and control (C2) and on the question of who commands globally-sourced air capabilities.

**A caveat on completeness.** The source material available for this synthesis covers only the front matter and opening chapters of each publication — roughly the first seven pages of each. AFDP 3-0.1's own table of contents shows that substantial content on the C2 process, C2 systems, the theater air control system, C2 technology, and four appendices lies beyond the excerpt reviewed here[^afdp-3-0-1-p2], and AFDP 3-36 likewise contains chapters on commanding mobility air forces and on planning that were not available[^afdp-3-36-p2]. Claims below are therefore limited to what appears in the reviewed pages; the absence of a topic here should not be read as its absence from the publications.

## The definition of command and control

Both publications use the same definition, which is the joint definition: command and control is the exercise of authority and direction by a properly designated commander over assigned and attached forces in the accomplishment of a mission[^afdp-3-0-1-p4][^afdp-3-36-p5].

AFDP 3-0.1 goes further and unpacks the compound term. C2 means something different from the two words that form it; individually, "command" and "control" describe authorities and responsibilities entrusted to a commander. In general, command is the authority and responsibility to lead an organization to accomplish a mission, and control is the authority that empowers a commander to employ forces to achieve that mission[^afdp-3-0-1-p4]. Taken together, "command and control" denotes the *act* of exercising authorities, and therefore encompasses four elements: a commander who exercises authority, a method for delegating authorities, the process that translates decisions into actions, and the systems that enable the direction of forces[^afdp-3-0-1-p4].

C2 is one of the seven joint functions — groupings of capabilities and activities that enable a joint force commander (JFC) to synchronize, integrate, and direct joint operations. AFDP 3-0.1 characterizes C2 as the *central* joint function because it affects and connects all the others: information, movement and maneuver, intelligence, fires, sustainment, and protection[^afdp-3-0-1-p4]. AFDP 3-36 approaches the same taxonomy from the other side, describing how rapid global mobility supports all the joint functions but especially C2, movement and maneuver, and sustainment[^afdp-3-36-p3].

## Mission command and the C2 framework

AFDP 3-0.1's foreword traces a deliberate doctrinal progression. In 2021 the USAF published AFDP 1, *The Air Force*, its first new capstone doctrine in six years; recognizing that the Service's increasingly centralized approach to operations was an ill fit for peer conflict, AFDP 1's most significant contribution was the addition of mission command as the central tenet of airpower[^afdp-3-0-1-p3]. Mission command was later refined in AFDP 1-1, *Mission Command*, as a philosophy of leadership that empowers Airmen to operate in uncertain, complex, and rapidly changing environments through trust, shared awareness, and understanding of commander's intent — a description drawing on lessons from sister Services whose adoption of mission command predates the USAF's own[^afdp-3-0-1-p3].

AFDP 3-0.1 presents mission command as implemented through the framework of **Centralized Command–Distributed Control–Decentralized Execution (CC-DC-DE)**[^afdp-3-0-1-p3]. A C2 framework is defined as the overarching approach to command relationships and authority delegation; the characteristics of the framework influence the act of C2 and shape the structure of C2 systems[^afdp-3-0-1-p7]. The implications of Distributed Control are the dominant focus of the publication and are what differentiate this revision from previous USAF treatments of C2[^afdp-3-0-1-p3].

The foreword frames Distributed Control as answering the question, "What is distributed, to whom, and for what purpose?" Its answer: (1) authority, (2) to subordinate commanders, (3) to conduct the C2 process[^afdp-3-0-1-p3]. The publication asserts this evolved approach is applicable to all USAF operations at every echelon of command[^afdp-3-0-1-p3].

AFDP 3-36 does not develop the CC-DC-DE framework, but it does list mission command first among the airpower tenets — alongside flexibility and versatility, synergistic effects, concentration, and priority — that have a direct impact on air mobility operations[^afdp-3-36-p5]. The two publications are consistent on this point; they simply operate at different levels of detail.

### Centralized command and unity of command

Centralized command gives the commander the responsibility and authority for planning, directing, and coordinating USAF forces for joint operations. It facilitates the development and delivery of all-domain effects requiring broad perspective, coordination, and reach, promoting effectiveness while preserving flexibility and versatility at the operational level, and supporting the joint principle of unity of command[^afdp-3-0-1-p7]. Unity of command means all forces operate under a single commander with the requisite authority to direct all forces employed in pursuit of a common purpose — a definition AFDP 3-0.1 uses to frame centralized command and to support the axiom "Airmen work for Airmen and the senior Airman works for the JFC"[^afdp-3-0-1-p7].

Critically, distribution of control does not dilute command. While the air component commander may distribute control of USAF forces to subordinate commanders to conduct operations, overall command responsibility for USAF assets remains under a single Airman, as expressed in the centralized command aspect of mission command and represented by the air component commander reporting directly to the JFC on matters of airpower[^afdp-3-0-1-p7].

## The commander: authorities and the decision cycle

The core element of C2 is the commander. Commanders use their authority to make decisions and direct action, and for air operations the air component commander has the authority, capability, and capacity to conduct the C2 process for assigned operations, balancing time between leading staffs through the C2 process and providing purpose, direction, and motivation to subordinate commanders and leaders[^afdp-3-0-1-p5].

### Delegated authorities

The air component commander's operational authorities are delegated from the JFC and are generally exercised in two hats: as commander, Air Force forces (COMAFFOR) over USAF forces, and as the functional joint force air component commander (JFACC) over joint air forces made available for tasking. JFCs generally delegate the COMAFFOR operational control (OPCON) and the JFACC tactical control (TACON)[^afdp-3-0-1-p5].

Authorities delegated to a JFACC are not limited to those specified under the definitions of OPCON and TACON. JFACCs are typically given additional authorities such as airspace control authority (ACA), and responsibilities such as area air defense commander (AADC). The net effect of these delegations is to make the air component commander the focal point of airpower C2 — leading USAF forces as the COMAFFOR and joint air operations as the JFACC[^afdp-3-0-1-p5].

### The decision cycle

Commanders drive the C2 process through a continuous cycle of understanding, visualizing, deciding, and directing, using the cycle to process information developed and refined throughout the C2 activities and to supply the decisions and directions that advance the process[^afdp-3-0-1-p5]. AFDP 3-0.1 explicitly notes this model is representative of other conceptual models such as Colonel John Boyd's observe-orient-decide-act (OODA) loop, and that regardless of the specific model, the purpose of any decision cycle is to make decisions with advantageous speed[^afdp-3-0-1-p5].

- **Understand.** Understanding is knowledge that has been synthesized and had judgment applied to comprehend the situation's inner relationships, enable decision-making, and drive action. Success demands timely and effective decisions based on applying judgment to available information and knowledge, so commanders and staffs seek to build and maintain situational understanding throughout an operation[^afdp-3-0-1-p5].
- **Visualize.** As commanders begin to understand their operational environment, they start visualizing a desired end-state and potential solutions. Commander's visualization is the mental process of developing situational understanding, determining a desired end-state, and envisioning an operational approach by which the force will achieve it; commanders generally accomplish visualization during design activities[^afdp-3-0-1-p6].
- **Decide.** Timely decisions and actions are essential for effective C2. Commanders who demonstrate the agility to consistently make appropriate decisions faster than their opponents have a significant advantage by dictating the operational tempo and seizing initiative[^afdp-3-0-1-p6].
- **Direct.** Commanders communicate intent and provide direction to convert decisions into actions, with plans and orders as the primary means; communicating direction contributes to the mission command principle of building shared understanding among subordinates[^afdp-3-0-1-p6].

AFDP 3-0.1 adds a note on the economy of the commander's own time: in deciding when and where to direct subordinates, the key is for commanders to determine where they can best use their limited time to the greatest effect — where their personal intervention will pay the greatest dividend[^afdp-3-0-1-p6].

The OODA construct recurs in AFDP 3-36, though applied to force posture rather than to an individual commander's cognition: Agile Combat Employment (ACE) is described as positioning USAF forces to observe, orient, decide, and act in concert across all domains[^afdp-3-36-p6]. This is a thematic echo rather than a cross-reference; the two publications do not cite each other on this point in the material reviewed.

### Battle rhythm

Decision cycles occur at different speeds based on the event horizons for their respective operations, and a battle rhythm integrates those cycles onto a single time schedule to support the commander at the required speed[^afdp-3-0-1-p6]. The air component commander's battle rhythm is a logical arrangement of boards, centers, cells, and working groups or activities, each with a clearly defined purpose and outcome. The JFC establishes a battle rhythm for joint operations, and the air component commander and subordinate commanders nest their component battle rhythm as appropriate[^afdp-3-0-1-p6].

At the theater level, the air operations center (AOC) director and the Air Force forces (AFFOR) chief of staff often collaborate to develop a synchronized battle rhythm that gives the commander a timeline for receiving critical information and establishing set decision points. Subordinate echelons and units of action should likewise create a battle rhythm, managed by the chief of staff, to integrate A-Staff activities[^afdp-3-0-1-p6].

## Air mobility: what is being commanded

AFDP 3-36 defines air mobility as the rapid movement of resources to, from, or within a theater by air. It constitutes one element of the strategic mobility triad — strategic airlift, strategic sealift, and pre-positioned stocks — which together provide the air, sea, and land infrastructure of the Defense Transportation System supporting DoD's transportation capability for the joint force[^afdp-3-36-p3].

Operations are categorized as **intertheater** (between two or more geographic areas of responsibility) or **intratheater** (exclusively within one AOR), and effective integration and synchronization of the two is described as crucial to positioning joint forces to a position of advantage[^afdp-3-36-p3]. This inter/intra distinction turns out to be the hinge for the command relationship questions discussed below.

Air mobility operations are an extension of airpower — the ability to project military power through control and exploitation in, from, and through the air — contributing by creating effects at all levels of warfare and breaking down geographical boundaries to apply force rapidly against many facets of an adversary's sources of power[^afdp-3-36-p3].

### The four core functions

DoD requires the USAF to provide the function of rapid global mobility to employ and sustain military forces that enable JFCs to conduct decisive operations across the competition continuum. To fulfill it, air mobility operations are classified into four core functions[^afdp-3-36-p3]:

- **Airlift** — the movement of personnel and materiel via mobility air forces (MAF) to support strategic, operational, and tactical objectives, providing rapid, flexible, and secure transportation; personnel and cargo, categorized as requirements, are transported to meet the JFC's objectives and priorities[^afdp-3-36-p4].
- **Air refueling (AR)** — the in-flight transfer of fuel from a tanker to a receiver aircraft in support of strategic, operational, and tactical objectives, expanding commanders' options by increasing the range, payload, persistence, and flexibility of joint and coalition receiver aircraft[^afdp-3-36-p4].
- **Aeromedical evacuation (AE)** — the movement of patients under medical supervision to and between medical treatment facilities by air, providing time-sensitive in-flight care to and between levels of care, predominantly using mobility aircraft or contracted civilian air ambulance aircraft with trained medical aircrew onboard[^afdp-3-36-p4].
- **Air mobility support** — the C2, aerial port, maintenance, and ground support capabilities for MAF operating worldwide, provided through the Global Air Mobility Support System (GAMSS), which consists of a limited number of permanent en route support locations plus ready deployable forces that augment existing locations or establish new ones[^afdp-3-36-p5].

### Operation ALLIES REFUGE as an integrated case

AFDP 3-36 uses Operation ALLIES REFUGE (OAR) to show all four core functions operating simultaneously. Over 17 days at the end of August 2021, nearly 800 civilian and military aircraft from more than 30 nations evacuated thousands of people from Afghanistan through Hamid Karzai International Airport (HKIA) in Kabul; the airlift spanned nine countries, eight time zones, and more than 10 temporary safe havens, becoming the largest non-combatant evacuation airlift in U.S. history[^afdp-3-36-p4].

More than 250 USAF mobility aircraft contributed, including all platforms of the airlift and air refueling fleet. Nearly 100 contingency response Airmen ran airfield operations at HKIA, unloading, repairing, and loading 721 of the 778 aircraft that transited the field and servicing an average of four aircraft simultaneously around the clock; they also repaired radars, airfield lighting, refueling capabilities, ground servicing equipment, and vehicles so HKIA could handle the influx of traffic[^afdp-3-36-p4]. Aeromedical evacuation personnel provided critical medical care en route, conducting multiple life-saving resuscitations and delivering three babies while airborne[^afdp-3-36-p4]. In total, the operation required all the air mobility core functions at a speed and scale never encountered before and supported the rapid evacuation of more than 124,000 people[^afdp-3-36-p4].

## Where the two publications meet

### Air mobility as an enabler of C2 itself

The most direct point of contact between the two documents is AFDP 3-36's treatment of C2 as a joint function. Rapid global mobility contributes to the C2 function through C2 elements operating within a unique Service C2 system; in this context, GAMSS forces may often serve as the initial C2 elements for deploying forces, and as mobility aircraft move and maneuver forces, they enable rapid and scalable growth of the overall C2 system[^afdp-3-36-p5].

This is a notable complement to AFDP 3-0.1's account. Where AFDP 3-0.1 treats C2 systems as one of the four elements of C2 — the systems that enable the direction of forces[^afdp-3-0-1-p4] — AFDP 3-36 supplies a mechanism by which such a system physically arrives and expands in theater. The reviewed excerpt of AFDP 3-0.1 does not itself discuss GAMSS, though its table of contents indicates a full chapter on C2 systems that was not available for review[^afdp-3-0-1-p2].

### Command relationships for globally-sourced capability

Both publications address, from opposite directions, the problem of commanding capabilities that originate outside a single combatant commander's AOR.

AFDP 3-0.1 states that centralized command of airpower facilitates the integration and synchronization of global USAF capabilities that may originate from outside a combatant commander's area of responsibility, and that the air component commander usually serves as the integrator for functional USAF forces from combatant commands without a defined AOR, naming USTRANSCOM as an example[^afdp-3-0-1-p7]. (The reviewed excerpt of AFDP 3-0.1 breaks off mid-sentence at this point, so any further examples or qualifications it offers are not captured here.)

AFDP 3-36 states the corresponding preference from the mobility side, under the principle of economy of force: because air mobility operations have a global impact, the preferred command relationship for intertheater MAF is for USTRANSCOM to support combatant commanders with defined AORs. However, under certain circumstances, the C2 of air mobility aircraft performing multi-role missions on the same sortie should be vested in one authority — normally the theater commander of Air Force forces[^afdp-3-36-p6].

These two statements are complementary rather than contradictory: AFDP 3-0.1 describes the theater air component commander as integrator for non-AOR functional forces[^afdp-3-0-1-p7], while AFDP 3-36 identifies the default supporting relationship for intertheater mobility and the specific multi-role case in which control consolidates under the theater COMAFFOR[^afdp-3-36-p6]. The reviewed material does not, however, provide a worked reconciliation of the two, and readers should consult the unreviewed chapters — particularly AFDP 3-36's Chapter 3, "Commanding Mobility Air Forces"[^afdp-3-36-p2] — before drawing firm conclusions about how integration and the supporting relationship interact in a given case.

### Strategic context

AFDP 3-0.1 situates its treatment of C2 explicitly in the context of great power competition (GPC), stating that it articulates C2 in the context of mission command to enable the USAF to adapt its force presentation in response to GPC and to facilitate joint all-domain operations (JADO), providing a common language and characterization for C2 aligned with Distributed Control[^afdp-3-0-1-p4]. Its foreword frames the most pressing objective for USAF doctrine as equipping the Service with the intellectual tools to prepare and posture for conflict in an era of great power competition[^afdp-3-0-1-p3].

AFDP 3-36 does not use the GPC framing in the reviewed pages, but it does address the contested-environment problem through ACE. ACE is described as a proactive and reactive scheme of maneuver executed within threat timelines to increase survivability while generating airpower; air mobility is a critical enabler, with MAF moving and maneuvering forces to predetermined, dispersed locations and flowing forces back to enduring locations[^afdp-3-36-p6]. The maneuver between enduring and contingency locations is intended to enhance mission-generation efficiency, increase survivability, and simplify sustainment, and the speed, range, and flexibility of MAF can provide meaningful maneuver for the air component and the entire joint force in contested, degraded, or operationally limited environments[^afdp-3-36-p6].

## Where the two publications do not overlap

Several topics appear in only one of the two documents within the reviewed material:

**Unique to AFDP 3-0.1.** The CC-DC-DE framework and the Distributed Control question[^afdp-3-0-1-p3]; the four-part decomposition of C2 into commander, delegation method, process, and systems[^afdp-3-0-1-p4]; COMAFFOR/JFACC dual-hatting and the OPCON/TACON, ACA, and AADC authorities[^afdp-3-0-1-p5]; the understand-visualize-decide-direct decision cycle[^afdp-3-0-1-p5][^afdp-3-0-1-p6]; and battle rhythm construction[^afdp-3-0-1-p6]. AFDP 3-0.1's foreword also records a deliberate content migration: the role of the COMAFFOR, force presentation and command relationships, and the distinct roles and responsibilities of organizations within an AOC are now addressed in AFDP 3-0, *Operations*, or remain in their respective tactical source documents, and AFDP 3-0.1 presents entirely new content in their place[^afdp-3-0-1-p3]. Readers looking for those topics should therefore expect to find them elsewhere.

**Unique to AFDP 3-36.** The strategic mobility triad and Defense Transportation System context[^afdp-3-36-p3]; the definitions of the four core functions[^afdp-3-36-p4][^afdp-3-36-p5]; and the application of joint-operations principles to mobility. On the latter, AFDP 3-36 identifies five principles of joint operations — mass, maneuver, economy of force, security, and surprise — as guiding the application of airpower through air mobility operations[^afdp-3-36-p5]. It elaborates that air mobility concentrates the effects of combat power at the most advantageous place and time, with mass often obtained through AR, which increases the range, payload, and persistence of receiving aircraft and acts as a force multiplier that significantly expands available combat power[^afdp-3-36-p6]. Robust air mobility operations keep adversaries off balance by rapidly repositioning forces, and air mobility is also key to exploiting successes and preserving freedom of action by rapidly adjusting lines of communication[^afdp-3-36-p6]. Under economy of force, MAF are characterized as high-demand, low-density assets that commanders should allocate to expend maximum possible combat power on primary effects, with the explicit warning that effectiveness should not be sacrificed for the sake of efficiency[^afdp-3-36-p6]. The discussion of security in the reviewed excerpt is truncated and states only that air mobility prevents the enemy from acquiring an unexpected advantage by moving forces outside the enemy's reach or expectation; the sentence is cut off in the available text and should be checked against the full publication[^afdp-3-36-p7].

AFDP 3-36 also distinguishes two sustainment modes: routine sustainment operations, which move materiel and personnel to reinforce or resupply already-deployed forces or support humanitarian relief organizations and typically employ channel airlift missions; and combat sustainment operations, which move supplies, materiel, and personnel to reinforce or resupply units already engaged in combat, for example by airland or airdrop delivery to combat zones[^afdp-3-36-p5]. Its treatment of movement and maneuver likewise separates movement — deploying or relocating forces without an expectation of contact with the enemy — from maneuver, the employment of forces for offensive and defensive purposes while in, or expecting, contact[^afdp-3-36-p5]. Airlift enhances deployment of critical early entry force packages over strategic distances without delays caused by terrain or obstacles, while AR extends range and expedites the arrival of self-deploying aircraft, precluding the need for intermediate staging bases[^afdp-3-36-p5].

Finally, AFDP 3-36 notes the role of non-organic and reserve contributions: combined with the effort of civilian air transportation partners and the total force integration of Regular and Air Reserve Component forces, the joint principles and airpower tenets help translate air mobility functions into operational concepts that exploit the airpower attributes of speed, range, and flexibility[^afdp-3-36-p5]. The reviewed pages of AFDP 3-0.1 do not address civilian or reserve force presentation.

## Summary

Read together, the two publications describe a division of labor. AFDP 3-0.1 supplies the grammar of command — the definition of C2, the commander at its core, the authorities that are delegated and distributed, the cycle by which decisions are made, and the framework (CC-DC-DE) that governs how far authority travels[^afdp-3-0-1-p3][^afdp-3-0-1-p4][^afdp-3-0-1-p5]. AFDP 3-36 supplies a major category of capability that is commanded through that grammar, while also being one of the means by which command itself is physically projected forward[^afdp-3-36-p3][^afdp-3-36-p5]. The shared touchpoints — the common C2 definition, the OODA-family decision construct, the mission command tenet, and the USTRANSCOM/theater-component command relationship question — are the places where a reader of one document should reach for the other.
